figures.alt: A single canvas with sixteen labeled casta panels, each showing a family of mixed ancestry with its category name.
figures.caption: Casta painting containing a complete set of 16 casta combinations (racial classifications in the Spanish colonies), 18th century, oil on canvas.

books.section: Topic 1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
The Social Structure of Spanish America
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: The paintings show too few ancestry combinations to represent colonial society.
options.misconception: Treats a complete catalog as too small a sample.

options.text: The paintings were made by Indigenous artists, so they show a Native view of the system.
The paintings prove the casta system stayed exactly the same from 1500 to 1800.
options.misconception: Treats a later source as proof of continuity.

options.text: The paintings show the system in the 1700s, a century after the period in question.

rationales.A: Sixteen panels cover every ancestry combination in the system, from Español con India to Tornaatras. Coverage is not the problem; the paintings are a complete catalog.
rationales.B: Spanish families in Mexico commissioned these paintings, not Indigenous artists. The canvas shows a Spanish view of the hierarchy, not a Native one.
rationales.C: One later source cannot prove that nothing changed. The casta system developed over the 1600s; the paintings show its later form, not its original one.
rationales.D: The canvas dates to the 1700s, while the student is writing about 1500 to 1607. The paintings show the casta system as it looked a century after that period, when the categories had multiplied and the hierarchy had hardened. A source can only speak directly for its own time; using an 18th-century painting to describe the early 1500s mistakes a later picture for an early one. The paintings are strong evidence for the 1700s, and weak evidence for the period they postdate.
rationales.general:
1. Check the date. The canvas is 18th-century work; the period in question ends in 1607.
2. Ask what the date means. The paintings show the system as it looked in the 1700s, not as it looked a century earlier.
3. Ask what the other options claim. Coverage is complete, the paintings were commissioned by Spanish families, and one later source cannot prove nothing changed.
4. Name the limit. A source speaks for its own time; this one postdates the period by a century.
Remember: a source's date is part of its evidence; ask what the source can show about its own time before using it for another.

stimulus.source_note: Casta painting, 18th century, oil on canvas, public domain; Wikimedia Commons.
stimulus.text: This single canvas gathers sixteen casta paintings, each labeling a different combination of parents and child. The panels run from 'Español con India, Mestizo' to 'Noteentiendo con India, Tornaatras,' covering Spanish, Indigenous, African, and mixed ancestry in every combination.
